summary: Selection is a free, fast, deterministic two-stage step: TypeScript groups candidates into events (Jev duplicate links at any age inside the read windows; same canonical URL or headline Jaccard >= 0.6 with >= 2 shared tokens within 72 h), and the SQL function marketing_dneskai_finish validates the grouping structurally and picks at most 4 events ordered by category_rank first, then Jev relevance, then publishedAt. The 4 cap is real in the schema (rank 1-4, unique(run_id,rank), selected_count 0-4). The owner brief's map matches the code on every rule it states. The central defect is the ordering: one-per-category is a hard key above relevance and recency, and the evergreen categories (marketing, tool, ai-project) draw from a 30-day pool, so on any night where all five categories have one >= 0.85 item, news gets at most 2 of 4 slots and a 28-day-old 0.85 ai-project repo displaces a 0.98 news story (reproduced in PGlite against the real migration). Around it: a lapsed, never-published brief permanently covers its topic (reproduced), held candidates never return, there is no owner swap/re-run/release path (a manual run needs a Vercel env JSON scope and a secret), the Zdroje tab shows 'Nevybrano' with no category, relevance, age or reason and lists at most 12 other events, a run that finishes after Prague midnight selects nothing silently, and the headline rule misses reworded or differently numbered headlines so the same story can split into several events. Docs drift is small and mostly precision (Jev links 'at any age' versus the 7-day duplicate read, 'validates the grouping' meaning structural checks only).

facts.fact: Tokenisation: NFKD + mark stripping folds diacritics, lower-cases with 'en', keeps letters/digits joined by . - + (versions such as 0.5.1 or gpt-4o stay whole), drops single-character tokens unless numeric, removes English and Czech (diacritics-folded) function words; the stop list includes 'new', 'nove', 'novy', 'nova' and has duplicate entries; the `'s` strip never fires because the token regex excludes apostrophes (measured: "OpenAI's model" -> openai, model).

findings.title: Docs and owner map overstate two points: Jev links 'at any age' and 'the SQL validates the grouping'
findings.claim: docs/dneskai-briefs.md:27 and the owner brief say a Jev duplicate link joins reports regardless of time; the pure function does, but the store feeds it duplicates from the last 7 days only (the same doc lists this at line 55), so an older link is never seen. The docs' eligibility list omits the `reason is null` and `publishedAt <= now` conditions, and its timing note (3000 reports in about half a second) is seven times slower than measured (70 ms).

findings.title: A single 22:00 cut-off and one run per date mean US-evening news reaches the feed a day and a half later
findings.claim: Collection is not due before 22:00 Prague and the schema allows one run per owner/project/date, so anything published after about 21:30 Prague (the US afternoon, when most AI announcements land) is first eligible the next night and posted the day after that. findings.title: Tokeniser details: product names stripped as Czech stop words, dead apostrophe handling, duplicated entries
findings.claim: 'nova', 'novy', 'nove' and 'new' are stop words, so 'Amazon Nova' becomes just 'amazon' and 'New York'/'New Relic' lose a token; the `'s` strip can never match because apostrophes are not part of the token regex; the stop list repeats 'a', 'i', 'so', 'than', 'now'. None is dangerous, but each weakens the only cheap grouping signal.

truth.evidence: dneskai-events.ts:51 lists nova/novy/nove and :41 new as stop words (probe: "Amazon Nova Premier launches" still matches "Amazon launches Nova Premier model" through other tokens); :57 token regex has no apostrophe, so the :58 's strip never matches; "than" and "now" appear twice in the English list (:42-44) and "a", "i", "so" in both lists.
